issue_paraphrase: Building ImmutableSet instances with a Builder that was created with an expected size, and then reusing that same Builder to build additional sets, can corrupt the builder's internal hash table. The first build shrinks the table to fit its contents, but the builder keeps using thresholds for the old larger table; after a few more elements are added, membership checks on the freshly built set can enter an infinite loop - a simple contains() call never returns - or, in other variants, silently lose or misreport elements. The problem shows up specifically when a single Builder is reused to build more than one set and the intermediate element counts hit certain sizes.
fix_summary: RegularSetBuilderImpl.review(), which shrinks the open-addressed hash table before build(), now also resets maxRunBeforeFallback and expandTableThreshold to values matching the new (smaller) table size instead of leaving the stale thresholds from the large initial table. With correct thresholds, subsequent adds either probe the small table correctly (falling back to the JDK-HashSet-backed builder once a run is exhausted) and build() no longer hands out a full table whose linear-probe contains() can spin forever.
notes: The parent failure mode is an INFINITE LOOP (the regression test hangs), so any oracle must run the test under a timeout and treat a timeout as the parent-side failure; the direct repro (a single contains(4) call with timeout) is the cleanest check. Whole guava/src compiles with plain javac in ~60-90s at 32 CPUs; no Maven, no network at test runtime. The JUnit3-style golden method runs without other ImmutableSetTest methods (RunOne harness instantiates the TestCase, setName() to the method, run()). The commit also carries Android/GWT twins of the change (android/guava/src/..., guava-gwt/test/...) which are not needed. ImmutableSetTest.java is not the only test class touched - guava-gwt/test/.../ImmutableSetTest_gwt.java is a generated wrapper; ignore it. The golden test compiles with just guava/src + guava-testlib/src + the two guava-tests files (ImmutableSetTest.java, AbstractImmutableSetTest.java) - no other guava-tests files needed.

observed_failure_at_parent: ByteSource.concat().slice(0, 3).slice(4, 3) throws IllegalArgumentException: 'length (-1) may not be negative' instead of returning an empty ByteSource. Golden test testSlice_returnEmptySource (overlaid from fix commit) errors at parent with the same message (JUnit3 RunOne output: 'TEST ... testSlice_returnEmptySource runCount=1 failures=0 errors=1; ERROR: ... length (-1) may not be negative'). Buggy code confirmed at parent by inspection: SlicedByteSource.slice() (ByteSource.java ~line 533) reads 'return ByteSource.this.slice(this.offset + offset, Math.min(length, maxLength));' with no maxLength<=0 guard, so when offset exceeds the slice length, min() yields -1 and the public slice() checkArgument(length >= 0) throws.
verified: Both directions observed in container 'mine-guava' on bench-base:ubuntu-24.04 (openjdk-21.0.12, javac). Fix presence confirmed: SlicedByteSource.slice() now reads 'return maxLength <= 0 ? ByteSource.empty() : ByteSource.this.slice(this.offset + offset, Math.min(length, maxLength));'.

issue_paraphrase: Calling slice() twice on a byte source can crash with an IllegalArgumentException instead of yielding an empty byte source. The documented semantics say that a slice whose requested region falls completely beyond the end of the source you are slicing should simply produce an empty byte source - in particular, slicing a byte source that is itself already a slice, with the second offset past the first slice's length, is documented to return an empty source. Instead the operation throws an exception complaining about a negative length, so code that defensively slices byte sources can fail at runtime on inputs where the docs promise an empty result.
fix_summary: SlicedByteSource.slice() now checks whether the requested offset is past the end of the current slice (maxLength <= 0) and, if so, returns ByteSource.empty() instead of recursing into slice(offset+offset, -1) which tripped the length>=0 precondition. Two-line change in guava/src/com/google/common/io/ByteSource.java (and the android/guava twin), plus the new regression test testSlice_returnEmptySource.
notes: Self-contained and fast: whole guava/src compiles with plain javac in ~60-90s; the reproduction needs no network, no Maven, no filesystem fixtures (ByteSource.concat() is an empty in-memory source). The golden test class ByteSourceTest requires the io test-dir closure listed in reproduction to compile (JUnit3-style; RunOne runs only the single method, so the class's other ~40 tests are not executed - the whole class is green at the fix commit, only testSlice_returnEmptySource fails at the parent). Direct repro is the fastest oracle: exit code plus stdout line. The 26MB io test-dir closure compiles in a few seconds.

dependency_pins.truth: 0.28 ONLY for the golden test compile+run - the 2016 commit's pom pins truth 0.28; any newer truth calls Strings.lenientFormat, which did not exist in 2016 guava, and the golden test then dies with NoSuchMethodError instead of running (observed with truth 0.44). install_recipe: Same javac-only recipe as the other entries, with ONE critical difference: use truth-0.28.jar (https://repo.maven.apache.org/maven2/com/google/truth/truth/0.28/truth-0.28.jar) - the version guava's own pom pinned in Oct 2016 - instead of 0.44, or the golden test fails with NoSuchMethodError on Strings.lenientFormat regardless of the bug being present. Direct repro does not need truth. Everything else identical: apt-get install openjdk-21-jdk, curl the jars, javac guava/src (+ guava-testlib/src for the golden test) + SplitterTest.java + AndroidIncompatible.java.
issue_paraphrase: Splitting a string with a regular expression that is capable of zero-width matches - like a word boundary or a lookahead/lookbehind - can silently drop the final character (or the entire string) from the result. A single-character input split on a word boundary comes back as an empty list instead of a one-element list, and a string like 'foo' split on lookarounds that should produce f, o, o comes back as f, o. The JDK's own String.split handles the same patterns correctly, so users switching between the two APIs get different results, and any code relying on the split output loses the last token without an error.
fix_summary: PatternSplitter's empty-match handling changes 'if (offset >= toSplit.length()) offset = -1;' to 'if (offset > toSplit.length()) offset = -1;'. Previously, when a zero-width match occurred exactly at the final position of the string, iteration stopped without a final separator search, so the trailing substring (the last character, or the whole string when the input is a single character) was dropped. With the relaxed condition the iterator does one more separatorStart() round, finds the end-of-string zero-width match, and emits the final token.
notes: Oldest entry (Oct 2016, guava ~19.x era; the issue itself is from 2012, moved from Google Code - do not assume the current master reflects this layout; the parent commit is what matters). Direct repro needs only guava/src (no testlib, no truth) and is the most robust oracle; use it as the primary check and the golden single-char test as the project-native check. The 2016 source compiles cleanly with javac 21. Dependency trap documented above: truth must be 0.28 for this era. Golden test class SplitterTest needs only guava-testlib/src (for NullPointerTester) + the one same-dir AndroidIncompatible.java annotation. Whole-guava compile ~60-90s at 32 CPUs; no network at test runtime.

issue_paraphrase: Asking an undirected graph built with the GraphBuilder API for its set of edges can return a set that violates the standard Collection contract: the set claims to contain an EndpointPair whose endpoints were passed in ordered form, but none of the pairs actually in the set equals that ordered pair. Code that relies on contains() to mean 'an equal element is present' - for example iterating the set to find the matching pair - therefore fails or returns nothing, and the same inconsistency appears across the graph/network APIs whenever an ordered endpoint pair is used with an undirected graph. The behavior is also asymmetric: on directed graphs the pair types are rejected, but on undirected graphs they slip through and produce these false-positive membership results.
fix_summary: EndpointPair ordering is now checked symmetrically: AbstractBaseGraph.isOrderingCompatible and AbstractNetwork.isOrderingCompatible change from 'endpoints.isOrdered() || !this.isDirected()' to 'endpoints.isOrdered() == this.isDirected()', so an undirected graph rejects ordered EndpointPairs (and a directed graph rejects unordered ones) with IllegalArgumentException(ENDPOINTS_MISMATCH); GraphConstants.ENDPOINTS_MISMATCH's message was generalized ('endpoints' ordering is not compatible with directionality of the graph') to cover both directions. AdjacentNode, edges/incidentEdges, hasEdgeConnecting(EndpointPair), edgeValueOrDefault(EndpointPair), putEdgeValue(EndpointPair,...) and the Network equivalents now refuse or correctly report the mismatched pair instead of returning false positives; the test suite's assertions were inverted to match (e.g. hasEdgeConnecting_undirected_mismatch now expects false, and edgesConnecting/edgeConnectingOrNull expect the exception).
notes: Newest entry (May 2022, guava 31.x era) and the only graph-package one; adds era diversity alongside the 2016 (Splitter), 2019 (ImmutableSet) and 2020 (ByteSource) fixes. Direct repro needs just guava/src (graph + base + collect + primitives) compiled with javac; no test framework at runtime. Caveat: this is a deliberate API behavior tightening (ordered pairs on undirected graphs go from silently accepted to rejected/false), so the task instruction must be phrased around the observable contract violation (contains() returning true with no equal element) rather than 'make the tests pass on new behavior', because at the fix commit existing user code calling putEdgeValue(EndpointPair.ordered(...)) on an undirected graph will start throwing. The golden classes live in the big graph test-suite hierarchy (AbstractGraphTest etc. in guava-testlib), which I did not compile; a task built on this entry should use the direct repro (or the small EndpointPairTest.endpointPair_undirected_contains method, which only needs the graph test dir + testlib) as the oracle.
